newsitem.title: USA: House panel clears Washington revitalization plan.
newsitem.headline: House panel clears Washington revitalization plan.

text.p: Most of a multibillion-dollar plan backed by President Clinton to revitalize the financially ailing District of Columbia won quick approval from a key House panel Thursday.
The District of Columbia subcommittee, headed by Virginia Republican Tom Davis, took less than 30 minutes to clear the 237-page blueprint for the District.
But the proposed National Capital Revitalization Act of 1997 faces major hurdles in other House and Senate committees in the months ahead.
"We pass one hurdle today, with many more to come before this plan becomes law," Eleanor Holmes Norton, the District's delegate to Congress, said.
"It will take a major effort by all concerned to get the city what it deserves. I am prepared to fight," she told the panel.
The bill would hand over to the federal government funding of billions of dollars in pension costs, Medicaid bills and prison financing now handled by the District.

The city assumed responsibility for those costs from the federal government when it won home rule in the 1970s. But ballooning costs, surburban flight and government mismanagement have left the city poverty-stricken, unable to to pay mounting bills or provide basic services.
"This is the moment of truth," Davis said, noting that Congress had only a few months to complete work on the bill.
"Precious time is running out," he said, calling the measure a "rare opportunity" to save the District.

Norton said the bill included an important "sleeper" provision that would let the city borrow up to $500 million over the next 15 years from the Treasury to pay off its massive deficit and use for short-term emergencies.

She said the measure dropped Clinton's proposal that the Internal Revenue Service take over tax collection for the city. Also gone would be a $125 million fund for the city to repair its roads and bridges.
The bill includes the president's plan for an Economic Development Corporation to spur jobs and businesses in poorer sections of the city.

The corporation would get $50 million in start-up costs, and it could hand out $75 million in tax credits. Businesses aided by the corporation could get $325 million in federal tax breaks over five years.
